category: Proper nouns, brand names, and words that lost their capital

examples: Aspirin is also used as a blood thinner.
She takes low-dose aspirin daily.
Aspirin is not recommended for children.
Take two aspirins and lie down.
Both aspirins had dissolved by then.

senses.head: The drug
examples: Aspirin is also used as a blood thinner.
She takes low-dose aspirin daily.
Aspirin is not recommended for children.

senses.head: Tablets
examples: Take two aspirins and lie down.
Both aspirins had dissolved by then.

entries.countability: uncountable as a drug; countable as tablets
entries.agreement: singular verb — aspirin is a blood thinner
entries.variants: generic in the United States; still a Bayer trademark in some countries
entries.contrast: Bayer lost the American trademark after the First World War, so aspirin is lowercase here. In Canada and Germany it is still Aspirin, capitalized. The generic chemical name is acetylsalicylic acid.

examples: Both escalators were out of order.
Take the escalator to the third floor.
The mall's escalators run all day.
She fell on an escalator and broke her wrist.
The word was a trademark until 1950.

senses.head: The machine
examples: Both escalators were out of order.
Take the escalator to the third floor.
The mall's escalators run all day.
She fell on an escalator and broke her wrist.
The word was a trademark until 1950.

entries.agreement: plural verb — both escalators were out of order
entries.variants: generic — the trademark was cancelled in 1950
entries.contrast: Otis lost the trademark precisely because the company's own advertising used the word generically. A textbook case of how genericization happens.

examples: The zipper on my jacket keeps jamming.
Both zippers broke within a month.
He replaced the zipper himself.
Cheap zippers fail first.
The British call it a zip.

senses.head: The fastener
examples: The zipper on my jacket keeps jamming.
Both zippers broke within a month.
He replaced the zipper himself.
Cheap zippers fail first.
The British call it a zip.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the zippers keep jamming
entries.variants: generic; British English says zip
entries.contrast: Originally a B.F. Goodrich trademark for a boot that closed with the fastener. The name transferred to the fastener itself and lost protection.

entries.meaning: The insulated container for hot or cold drinks.
examples: He filled a thermos with coffee.
Both thermoses leaked in the backpack.
A good thermos keeps soup hot all day.
She packed two thermoses for the drive.
The neutral term is vacuum flask.

senses.head: The container
examples: He filled a thermos with coffee.
Both thermoses leaked in the backpack.
A good thermos keeps soup hot all day.
She packed two thermoses for the drive.
The neutral term is vacuum flask.

entries.agreement: plural verb — both thermoses leaked
entries.variants: generic in the United States since 1963; the neutral term is vacuum flask
entries.contrast: An American court ruled the word generic because the public used it as the name of the product rather than the brand. Elsewhere Thermos remains a trademark.

examples: Heroin is highly addictive.
The city's heroin problem worsened that decade.
Heroin was originally sold as a cough remedy.
Both seizures involved heroin and fentanyl.
The word was a Bayer trademark until 1919.

senses.head: The drug
examples: Heroin is highly addictive.
The city's heroin problem worsened that decade.
Heroin was originally sold as a cough remedy.
Both seizures involved heroin and fentanyl.
The word was a Bayer trademark until 1919.

entries.agreement: singular verb — heroin is highly addictive
entries.variants: generic — originally a Bayer trademark, like aspirin
entries.contrast: A homophone of heroine, the female hero — see hero. Bayer trademarked both Heroin and Aspirin, and lost both.

examples: The granola is homemade.
She puts granola on yogurt every morning.
Store-bought granola is mostly sugar.
It's a very granola part of town.
Both granolas on the shelf were organic.

senses.head: The food
examples: The granola is homemade.
She puts granola on yogurt every morning.
Store-bought granola is mostly sugar.

senses.head: Earnestly natural
examples: It's a very granola part of town.
Both granolas on the shelf were organic.

entries.countability: uncountable as food; countable as varieties
entries.agreement: singular verb — the granola is homemade
entries.variants: generic since the nineteenth century
entries.contrast: Also an American adjective meaning earnestly natural or hippie-ish: a very granola neighborhood.

examples: Both laundromats are open until midnight.
There's a laundromat on the corner.
She does her washing at the laundromat.
The building has no laundromat nearby.
The British word is launderette.

senses.head: The business
examples: Both laundromats are open until midnight.
There's a laundromat on the corner.
She does her washing at the laundromat.
The building has no laundromat nearby.
The British word is launderette.

entries.agreement: plural verb — both laundromats are open late
entries.variants: generic in the United States; British English says launderette
entries.contrast: Originally a Westinghouse trademark. Note the American/British split: laundromat versus launderette.

examples: The dumpsters behind the store were overflowing.
He threw the whole box in the dumpster.
Both dumpsters are emptied on Fridays.
The whole launch was a dumpster fire.
That meeting was an absolute dumpster fire.

senses.head: The container
examples: The dumpsters behind the store were overflowing.
He threw the whole box in the dumpster.
Both dumpsters are emptied on Fridays.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: The whole launch was a dumpster fire.
That meeting was an absolute dumpster fire.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the dumpsters were overflowing
entries.variants: largely generic in American use; originally the Dempster Brothers' Dumpster
entries.contrast: Now overwhelmingly lowercase in American writing. Note the extremely common figurative phrase a dumpster fire, meaning a chaotic disaster.

entries.meaning: The frozen flavored ice on a stick.
examples: The popsicles melted before we got home.
She had a grape popsicle.
Both popsicles broke off the stick.
Popsicles are the only thing he'll eat when sick.
The neutral term is ice pop.

senses.head: The frozen treat
examples: The popsicles melted before we got home.
She had a grape popsicle.
Both popsicles broke off the stick.
Popsicles are the only thing he'll eat when sick.
The neutral term is ice pop.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the popsicles melted
entries.variants: still a trademark (Popsicle), though used generically; the neutral term is ice pop or freezer pop
entries.contrast: Legally still owned by Unilever, so careful commercial writing says ice pop. In ordinary American speech everyone says popsicle, lowercase.

entries.meaning: The flat plastic disc thrown as a toy.
examples: Both frisbees ended up on the roof.
He threw the frisbee for the dog.
She brought a frisbee to the beach.
The sport's official name is ultimate.
Competitive players say disc, not frisbee.

senses.head: The disc
examples: Both frisbees ended up on the roof.
He threw the frisbee for the dog.
She brought a frisbee to the beach.
The sport's official name is ultimate.
Competitive players say disc, not frisbee.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the frisbees ended up on the roof
entries.variants: still a trademark (Frisbee, owned by Wham-O); the neutral term is flying disc
entries.contrast: The sport is officially ultimate, not ✗ ultimate frisbee, precisely because of the trademark. Competitive players say disc.

examples: Do you have a kleenex?
The kleenexes were all used up.
She went through half a box of kleenex.
He kept a packet of kleenex in the car.
The neutral word is tissue.

senses.head: The tissue
examples: Do you have a kleenex?
The kleenexes were all used up.
She went through half a box of kleenex.
He kept a packet of kleenex in the car.
The neutral word is tissue.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the kleenexes were all used up
entries.variants: still a trademark (Kleenex); the neutral term is tissue or facial tissue
entries.contrast: Kimberly-Clark actively defends this mark, so published writing says tissue. In American speech kleenex is the ordinary word for any brand, usually lowercase.

examples: Put a band-aid on it.
The band-aids kept falling off in the water.
She keeps band-aids in her desk.
The funding is a band-aid, not a solution.
Both proposals were band-aid fixes.

senses.head: The bandage
examples: Put a band-aid on it.
The band-aids kept falling off in the water.
She keeps band-aids in her desk.

senses.head: An inadequate temporary fix
examples: The funding is a band-aid, not a solution.
Both proposals were band-aid fixes.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the band-aids kept falling off
entries.variants: still a trademark (Band-Aid, Johnson & Johnson); the neutral term is adhesive bandage
entries.contrast: Extremely common figuratively: a band-aid solution means an inadequate temporary fix. That figurative use is always lowercase.

examples: Make three xeroxes of this page.
The xeroxes were completely unreadable.
She kept a xerox of every receipt.
Could you xerox this for me?
The neutral verb is photocopy.

senses.head: A photocopy
examples: Make three xeroxes of this page.
The xeroxes were completely unreadable.
She kept a xerox of every receipt.

senses.head: As a verb
examples: Could you xerox this for me?
The neutral verb is photocopy.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the xeroxes were unreadable
entries.variants: still a trademark (Xerox); the neutral terms are photocopy and copy
entries.contrast: Xerox campaigned publicly against using its name as a verb. Note the initial x is pronounced /z/, as in xylophone.

entries.meaning: To search the internet; also a search.
examples: Just google it.
She googled him before the interview.
I googled the symptoms and regretted it.
A quick google would have answered that.
Two googles later he had the address.

senses.head: As a verb
examples: Just google it.
She googled him before the interview.
I googled the symptoms and regretted it.

senses.head: As a noun
examples: A quick google would have answered that.
Two googles later he had the address.

entries.countability: countable as a search; usually a verb
entries.agreement: singular verb — a quick google is enough
entries.variants: still a trademark (Google); the neutral terms are search and web search
entries.contrast: The most recent major genericization in English. The verb entered dictionaries in 2006, and Google has fought to keep it capitalized as a noun while the lowercase verb to google is now completely standard.

entries.meaning: The fabric fastener of hooks and loops.
examples: The velcro on his shoes has worn out.
The strap closes with velcro.
Velcro loses its grip when it fills with lint.
Children's shoes often use velcro instead of laces.
The neutral term is hook-and-loop fastener.

senses.head: The fastener
examples: The velcro on his shoes has worn out.
The strap closes with velcro.
Velcro loses its grip when it fills with lint.
Children's shoes often use velcro instead of laces.
The neutral term is hook-and-loop fastener.

entries.agreement: singular verb — the velcro has worn out
entries.variants: still a trademark (Velcro); the neutral term is hook-and-loop fastener
entries.contrast: The company ran a widely shared video begging people to say hook and loop. Almost nobody does. The name is a blend of French velours and crochet.

entries.meaning: A bath or pool with underwater jets.
examples: Both jacuzzis were closed for maintenance.
The room has a jacuzzi on the balcony.
They sat in the jacuzzi until midnight.
Several jacuzzis line the pool deck.
Most Americans just say hot tub.

senses.head: The tub
examples: Both jacuzzis were closed for maintenance.
The room has a jacuzzi on the balcony.
They sat in the jacuzzi until midnight.
Several jacuzzis line the pool deck.
Most Americans just say hot tub.

entries.agreement: plural verb — both jacuzzis were closed
entries.variants: still a trademark (Jacuzzi); the neutral terms are hot tub and whirlpool bath
entries.contrast: Named for the Jacuzzi brothers, Italian immigrants to California. Hot tub is the ordinary American word.

examples: Hand me a sharpie.
All the sharpies had dried out.
She labeled every box with a sharpie.
Both sharpies bled through the paper.
The neutral term is permanent marker.

senses.head: The marker
examples: Hand me a sharpie.
All the sharpies had dried out.
She labeled every box with a sharpie.
Both sharpies bled through the paper.
The neutral term is permanent marker.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the sharpies dried out
entries.variants: still a trademark (Sharpie); the neutral term is permanent marker
entries.contrast: Thoroughly genericized in American speech, where a sharpie means any permanent marker regardless of brand.

examples: She left a post-it on my monitor.
All the post-its fell off the wall overnight.
His desk is covered in post-its.
Both post-its had the same phone number.
The neutral term is sticky note.

senses.head: The note
examples: She left a post-it on my monitor.
All the post-its fell off the wall overnight.
His desk is covered in post-its.
Both post-its had the same phone number.
The neutral term is sticky note.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the post-its fell off the wall
entries.variants: still a trademark (Post-it, 3M); the neutral term is sticky note
entries.contrast: Sticky note is the neutral term and is genuinely common, unlike some of the others in this group.

examples: The q-tips are in the medicine cabinet.
Use a q-tip to clean the lens.
Both q-tips came apart.
Doctors say not to put q-tips in your ears.
The neutral term is cotton swab.

senses.head: The swab
examples: The q-tips are in the medicine cabinet.
Use a q-tip to clean the lens.
Both q-tips came apart.
Doctors say not to put q-tips in your ears.
The neutral term is cotton swab.

entries.agreement: plural verb — the q-tips are in the cabinet
entries.variants: still a trademark (Q-tips); the neutral term is cotton swab
entries.contrast: In American English q-tip is simply the word for the object. The British say cotton bud.

examples: The styrofoam is not recyclable here.
The cups are styrofoam, unfortunately.
Packing styrofoam filled the whole box.
Several cities have banned styrofoam containers.
The neutral term is expanded polystyrene.

senses.head: The material
examples: The styrofoam is not recyclable here.
The cups are styrofoam, unfortunately.
Packing styrofoam filled the whole box.
Several cities have banned styrofoam containers.
The neutral term is expanded polystyrene.

entries.agreement: singular verb — the styrofoam is not recyclable
entries.variants: still a trademark (Styrofoam, Dow); the neutral term is expanded polystyrene or foam
entries.contrast: Strictly, the trademarked product is a rigid blue building insulation, not the white foam cups everyone calls Styrofoam. The everyday use is doubly generic.

entries.meaning: The third day of the week.
examples: The meeting is on Tuesday.
Tuesdays are always the busiest.
We close early on Tuesdays.
Both Tuesdays in April are holidays.
Write Tuesday in March, but spring with a small letter.

senses.head: The day
examples: The meeting is on Tuesday.
Tuesdays are always the busiest.
We close early on Tuesdays.
Both Tuesdays in April are holidays.

senses.head: Capitalization contrast
examples: Write Tuesday in March, but spring with a small letter.

entries.agreement: plural verb — Tuesdays are always busy
entries.contrast: Days and months are always capitalized in English, unlike in Russian, French, or Spanish. ✗ tuesday and ✗ january are errors. But seasons are not capitalized: spring, summer, fall, winter.

entries.meaning: The first month of the year.
examples: The contract starts in January.
Recent Januaries have been unusually mild.
Both Januaries set cold records.
She was born in January of 1998.
Capitalize January, but not winter.

senses.head: The month
examples: The contract starts in January.
Recent Januaries have been unusually mild.
Both Januaries set cold records.
She was born in January of 1998.

senses.head: Capitalization contrast
examples: Capitalize January, but not winter.

entries.agreement: plural verb — recent Januaries have been mild
entries.contrast: Capitalized, like all months and days. Note the plural takes -ies, since the word ends in a consonant plus y. Named for the Roman god Janus.
